name: Javanese
confidence_why: Older descriptions contradict one another (Poedjosoedarmo 1982 final stress, Ras 1985 penultimate unless it holds schwa, Horne 1961 no fixed rule), but the instrumental work of Stoel 2006, Goedemans & van Zanten 2007 and Schubö 2021 agrees that Javanese has no word-level stress and marks prominence by a pitch rise at the phrase edge, so the disagreement is real but the modern answer is clear.
catalog_citation: Stoel, Ruben (2006). The intonation of Banyumas Javanese. Proceedings of Speech Prosody 2006, Dresden (ISCA Archive), sec. 3 'Stress' and abstract; with Goedemans, R. & E. van Zanten (2007). Stress and accent in Indonesian. In van Zanten & Goedemans (eds), Pr…
catalog_locator: Stoel 2006: p.1, sec. 3 'Stress' (+ abstract, sec. 5.1); Goedemans & van Zanten 2007: printed p.41 (p.7); Ras 1985 via the StressTyp2 entry(no page).
catalog_quote: Stoel 2006 sec. 3: "There is no agreement among authors on the stress pattern of Javanese. Poedjosoedarmo [9] claims that Javanese has final stress, while Ras [10] states that stress falls on the penultimate syllable, but if it contains a schwa, then it is the final syllable that gets the stress. Horne [4], on the other hand, denies that there are any fixed rules for stress in Javanese, and claims that any syllable can get the main stress. Goedemans and van Zanten [2] present convincing evidence that, in Indonesian as spoken by a speaker of Javanese, there are no phonetic correlates for stress, and an accent on the penultimate or final syllable is equally acceptable for listeners. I assume that not only Indonesian as spoken by speakers of Javanese does not have stress, but that this is also the case for Javanese itself." ... sec. 5: "the H target of a non-final HL% tone is aligned with …

audit.recode_to: phrasal (no word stress; AP-final boundary tone, H aligned with penult or final syllable, schwa-penult favouring final) -- as Betawi (beta1252) is coded from the same LOT-school evidence; keep Ras's schwa rule as the alignment-tendency/legacy note.
audit.reasoning: Quote check: all three quoted passages (Stoel 2006 abstract/sec.3/sec.5.1; Goedemans & van Zanten 2007 p.41; the StressTyp2 entry= Ras 1985) are verbatim in copies we hold. Deciding source is a 2006 instrumental conference paper plus a 2007 experimental chapter; both. Web/API search (Crossref, ISCA archive indexes, IA; the newest work, Schubö 2021 (downloaded), treats 'Javanese lacks lexical stress and lexical tone' as established (citing G&vZ 2007, G&vZ 2014, van Zanten-Stoel-Remijsen 2010) and adds one-speaker production data with AP-final rises. van Heuven & van Zanten 2007:194 (downloaded) group Javanese with languages 'described as having weak stress' and suspect it lacks word stress. sources.quote: p.40: '...Perhaps the fact that in Java stress tends to be final and shortening of high frequency words often occurs ... had something to do with this.' p.49 fn.45: 'Stress in the Indonesian of some speakers is penultimate unless the penultimate vowel is /e/ [schwa], in which case the stress is final. In the Indonesian spoken in most of Java, however, stress is final as it is in Javanese and Sundanese.' Confirms first-hand the 'Poedjosoedarmo = final stress' leg that the record carried via Stoel and G&vZ (their locator p.49 fn.45 is exact).

sources.locator: sec. 2.3 'Word Order', printed p. 318; continues p. 319: 'The newest and most important information is signalled by a falling tone; The second most important l…
sources.note: A syntax paper (verb morphology, NP marking, word order, Old vs modern Javanese). Its only prosodic content is phrase-level intonation: each grammatical phrase is an information unit carried by a rising, falling(-rising) or flat contour, with the contours ordered rising > falling > flat and exactly one falling unit per utterance. Nothing is said about word stress, its position, secondary stress, syllable weight, schwa, or lexical tone in Javanese; the one mention of a 'stressed syllable' (p. 311) describes English focus marking. The phrasal-intonation account is compatible with the catalog's '
sources.venue: The history and typology of Western Austronesian voice systems

sources.citation: Ardini, Sukma Nur & Senowarsito, Senowarsito. 2023. Prosodic Features of Jonglish Community: An Effort to A Glocalization. Indonesian Journal of EFL and Linguistics 8(2): 379-394. doi:10.21462/ijefl.v8i2.676
sources.note: The article measures pitch and loudness of Javanese-accented English (Jonglish) against a native English speaker and finds no discernible difference; its only remark on stress is that Javanese speakers may stress different English syllables than native speakers, an L2-English observation. It states nothing about word stress, accent or tone in Javanese itself, so the catalog entry (phrasal, no tone) is untouched.
sources.venue: Indonesian Journal of EFL and Linguistics

sources.citation: Pinem, Yune Andryani & Nasution, Fauzia Fahmi Yuniarti. 2019. Stylistic Analysis of English Imperative Command Mood Transfer to Javanese. LLT Journal: A Journal on Language and Language Teaching 22(1): 11-22. doi:10.24071/llt.v22i1.1646
sources.note: The article measures sentence-level pitch range (max and min F0) of Javanese Ngoko and Krama imperatives and their English counterparts read by five Jogja-Solo speakers, finding Krama commands kept in a small, low pitch range and Ngoko/English ranges irregular. It says nothing about the position or existence of word stress or about lexical tone in Javanese, so it neither supports nor challenges the catalog's phrasal / no-tone entry.
sources.venue: LLT Journal: A Journal on Language and Language Teaching
